frame: A girl who moved to Twotide Atoll wrote this for the school magazine. The Pointern circled one bit.
text: I have always hated the sea. I want to be clear about that from the start. It is cold, it is wet, it is full of things that sting, and it tastes like a sock that has been pickled. When Mum announced that we were moving to Twotide Atoll, where the sea is everywhere you look, I locked myself in the bathroom for an entire afternoon. Our new house was so close to the water that I could hear it at night, shushing and grumbling, as if it were complaining about me. For the first month, I didn't go near it. Then, one evening, my little brother's kite blew out over the lagoon, and before I could think, I had waded in up to my knees to grab the string. The water was warm. That surprised me so much that I just stood there, holding the kite, while tiny silver fish nibbled at my ankles as if they were checking whether I was edible. A turtle surfaced a few metres away, looked at me with its old, wrinkled face and sank again without a sound. I stayed until the sun went down. I still think the sea tastes like a pickled sock. But now, every evening, I am the first one in the water, and Mum has to drag me out when it gets dark.

text: For two years, Sami and Leo built a video game called Tide Runners in Leo's garage, on a computer they had rescued from the tip. On stage, Sami held up the trophy and pointed at the big screen behind him, where Leo was cheering on a video call from the mainland, at six in the morning, still in his pyjamas. The crowd went wild. Afterwards, Sami walked home by himself, past Leo's old garage, which now had a FOR SALE sign on the door. text: Lena had been practising her trumpet solo for six months, and the audition for the State Youth Band was at ten o'clock. Only performers were allowed in the room, so I waited in the corridor outside, pacing up and down the squeaky lino and trying not to bite my nails. Every few minutes, I checked my watch. Through the heavy wooden door, I heard her start. The first few notes wobbled, then steadied, and then the solo soared, so loud and bright that the cleaner down the hall stopped mopping to listen. Then it stopped, halfway through a phrase. There was a long silence. I pressed my ear against the door, but all I could make out was a murmur of low voices, as if the three judges were whispering to each other. Ten minutes later, Lena came out holding her trumpet case in both arms. Her face gave nothing away. Even her ears, which go red when she's upset, were their normal colour. 'Well?' I said. She shrugged and said they'd send a letter. In the car on the way home, she stared out of the window and hummed the solo over and over, but every time I asked what the judges had whispered, she turned up the radio.
